articles.title: ‘Someone else will do it for less’: Refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay
articles.summary: Refugee gig workers for tech companies don’t know how much they’ll be paid – if AI hasn’t already taken their jobs. In a portable building in Kakuma, a refugee camp near Kenya ’s northern border with South Sudan, Grace used ChatGPT to research translations of Christian hymns in languages she…
body: Grace, who requested anonymity due to a nondisclosure agreement, prompted ChatGPT to translate the hymn’s English text into the assigned east Asian language. She then used the translation to search for existing versions and find information about its translator, author and Christian denomination. She fed those details to AOP Connect, a crowdsourced research platform owned by British AI enterprise software company RWS.

If RWS deems her work high quality based on six listed criteria, it could award her up to $500 as a “discretionary reward”, according to RWS researcher documents and manuals reviewed by the Guardian. But refugees aren’t guaranteed wages, and most earn significantly less than the maximum without being told why, said Asha Luka Abdallah, a mentor at the Solidarity Initiative for Refugees (SIR), an organization that trains refugees to work in the tech outsourcing industry.

Remote jobs such as content moderation and data annotation have been promoted as a win-win by United Nations agencies as well as global tech companies: refugees get income opportunities, AI and social media companies get a source of cheap labor.
points: Refugee gig workers for tech companies don’t know how much they’ll be paid – if AI hasn’t already taken their jobs.

articles.title: ‘Vibrant, design-led and surprisingly green’: why the Dutch city of Eindhoven is perfect for a relaxed arty break
articles.summary: After electronics giant Philips left, the city reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for creativity and innovation, and the home of Dutch Design Week. A baggily clad skateboarder’s wheels clatter across concrete floors, the noise bouncing off exposed pipes and iron girders.
body: I’m in the Dutch city of Eindhoven, in North Brabant, famous for its historic connection to Philips, the one-time electronics giant. The restaurant, Radio Royaal, is housed in what was once their engine room, in the Strijp-S neighbourhood. Today, Strijp-S buzzes with concept stores, an indoor food market, MU Hybrid Art House and the Area 51 skatepark. The broader area, Strijp, was where the company was largely headquartered: its zones are named S, T and R. In the late 90s, Philips withdrew from the city where it had started in 1891, and the letters I, J and P were never assigned.

Philips had employed about half of the region’s working population, so its departure for Amsterdam inevitably left a huge hole. Fortunately for Eindhoven, this was short-lived, and within a decade the city had reinvented itself as a multicultural hub for design and innovation – so much so that Dutch Design Week, the largest event of its kind in northern Europe, has been held here since 2005.

articles.title: You be the judge: my friend and I bought a tent but she’s moved away. Who owns it now?
articles.summary: Ava shared the initial cost but Ruth has forked out for repairs. You decide who’s on the wrong side of this in-tents debate? • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror. I paid for half of the tent, so I deserve equal use of it, even if we no longer live in the same country.
body: Ruth and I bought a tent together when we were living together in Spain and going to festivals there. We had a good time using it, and took it to four different festivals in Spain and Portugal. And after that we used it every year for festivals and camping trips.

It was always our tent, not Ruth’s tent that I occasionally borrowed. I moved back to the UK in 2024 and Ruth stayed in Spain, so it made sense for the tent to stay with her. There wasn’t much point in me taking half a tent back to London, and at the time there was no reason to formally decide who owned it. We were friends, we’d always used it together so I assumed it still belonged to both of us.

Now we both have partners and both need the tent. I’m coming back to Spain for a festival and asked Ruth if I could use the tent with my boyfriend Michael. The problem is that she’s going to the festival too with her partner, Luis, and wants it for herself.

articles.title: The dreadful decline of hosting at home: ‘I feel shame any time a friend comes over’
articles.summary: It used to be quite normal to pop next door for a coffee or invite friends over for dinner. But not any more. What’s behind this change – and just how damaging is it? ‘I really loved hosting at home years ago, before I had kids, when my house wasn’t filled with toys and I had lots of time to plan…
body: Personally, I’d never say no to a cold buffet – but Rehanna’s story is not unusual. In the US, the number of people who regularly host friends or family fell from 42% in 1975 to 12% in 2026 – a 70% drop over the last 50 years. In the UK, the numbers are not much better: last year, a poll of 2,000 adults found that more than four in 10 British people avoid hosting at home due to the clean-up it requires. And while chef Nigella Lawson is back on TV screens demonstrating her culinary prowess on The Great British Bake Off, it wasn’t long ago that the self-proclaimed domestic goddess revealed even she had “got out of the habit” of hosting formal dinner parties.
But why have we become so unwilling to invite others into our homes – and what do we lose by only catching up in communal “third spaces”?

articles.title: Just Browsing: Sézane’s Parisian Outpost on the Upper East Side
articles.summary: The French brand’s new Madison Avenue shop is designed to look like an artful apartment—take a peek inside, plus, browse the fall collection.
body: Manhattan’s Upper East Side is famously picturesque, but never is its charm offensive stronger than a weekday morning in early fall. The streets are relieved of their weekend park crowds; the sun is doing some of its best work. There’s now another good reason to plan a visit Uptown: Sézane’s newest store, a layered, vintage-inspired space that’s part showroom, part boutique, and recently opened on Madison Avenue.

It’s the brand’s third L’Appartement in New York, and the first U.S. retail project from Saint-Germain-des-Prés-based interior design studio Pierre Lacroix. Created in tandem with founder Morgane Sézalory, it was conceptualized to feel more like a Parisian home than a traditional retail space. The interiors do not disappoint—the fitting room opens with a bubblegum-pink velvet sofa and matching walls, the long display table in the main room is outfitted with design books and flowers, and there is vintage furniture everywhere.

articles.title: What Should You Do About Your First Gray Hairs?
articles.summary: When I got my first gray hairs, it became my mission to find a solution. Here are the tried-and-tested ways to shield or celebrate your grays—from semi-permanent color to smoothing glosses.
body: I wanted to get to the bottom of why this occurs. What causes gray hair, and why does it feel like a different texture? “Hair goes gray when your follicles, tiny pigment factories, start shutting down,” explains colorist Hannah Gayle, who is based out of Hershesons Belgravia. “When there is less melanin and less color, eventually, silver/white hairs appear; basically, your hair is saying, ‘I’m retiring from the dye department.’ Your DNA decides when your hair’s little pigment factories start clocking out, and when pigment production slows down, the follicle can change too. So gray hairs often grow coarser, drier, wirier and a little more unruly.”

Hair colorist Josh Wood adds that while the biggest factor is genetics, “There can also be other influences, including stress and overall health.” He adds that while some people “are lucky enough to develop beautifully soft, silky gray hair,” for others, “it can feel thicker, coarser, and a little more unruly.”

In my case, and most commonly, gray hair appears at the temples and hairline. Wood confirms this as the norm: “Generally, the pattern tends to start at the front and gradually work its way towards the back of the head.”

articles.title: The 28 Best Destination Wedding Guest Dresses for Every Exotic Locale
articles.summary: If you’re traveling for a loved one’s ceremony, consider Vogue’s edit of the best destination wedding guest dresses fit for any setting and theme.
body: The thrill of receiving a destination wedding save-the-date is twofold (provided it arrives well in advance). There’s the honor of being invited, of course, and then there’s the trip itself—a weekend away at a venue that doubles as a vacation spot. But there’s a sartorial perk, too: Destination wedding guest dresses are some of the most fun to wear, allowing you to borrow from the spirit of the location.

A countryside affair, for instance, calls for something that nods to the pastoral or, at the very least, florals. Headed to a rooftop ceremony in a far-flung city? Keep things modern and polished in Staud or Christopher John Rogers. Maybe you booked a puddle jumper to the New England coast? There’s no need to overhaul your style to embrace prep, though a touch of blue is a nice wink to your surroundings. Tropical getaways and beach nuptials, meanwhile, invite a hit of sequins and shine à la Tory Burch or a sunset-hued print by La DoubleJ. You get the picture—let the setting (and the dress code) lead, no matter where your invite takes you.
Ahead, we’ve rounded up 28 destination wedding guest dresses that are as striking as the venues themselves.

articles.title: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You
articles.summary: This misunderstood spud can turn into all sorts of healthy—and filling—dinners.
body: Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

While you can’t scroll through a healthy-recipe collection without seeing a sweet potato or three, you’d be hard-pressed to find white potatoes like russets included on most lists. These spuds are often seen as bad for you, while their orange-hued brethren have taken on a health halo. But why? When you look at the nutrition facts, the two are nearly identical.

“Diets like keto and Atkins, and the recent TikTok protein craze can promote the idea that carbs drive weight gain or that they provide empty calories,” says Hannah Sorrell, a registered dietitian at Alike Nutrition. “However, carbohydrates are our brain and body’s main fuel source.” What’s more, Sorrell notes that carbs are also the only macronutrient that contain fiber (a large russet brings about four grams if eaten skin-on).
points: This misunderstood spud can turn into all sorts of healthy—and filling—dinners.
